title: Kanpur BTech Gold Medallist Dies by Suicide After 50 Failed Government Job Attempts
excerpt: A young engineering graduate's heartbreaking farewell note — 'Sorry papa, I tried' — exposes the crushing toll of India's broken government hiring system on its most qualified youth.
body:
• A BTech gold medallist from Kanpur died by suicide after failing to secure a government job despite appearing for more than 50 competitive examinations.
  • The young man left a suicide note addressed to his father saying 'Sorry papa, I tried,' drawing nationwide attention to India's unemployment crisis among educated youth.
  • India's government job vacancy pipeline remains severely choked, with millions of candidates competing for a fraction of available positions each year.
  • The tragedy adds to a growing list of suicides linked to examination pressure and unemployment, prompting renewed calls for mental health support and recruitment reform.

A BTech gold medallist from Kanpur, Uttar Pradesh, has died by suicide after failing to secure a government job despite sitting for more than 50 competitive examinations, police said on Friday. The young man left behind a handwritten note addressed to his father that read, "Sorry papa, I tried" — words that have since ricocheted across Indian social media and reignited a fierce debate over the country's broken public-sector hiring system.

A Promising Graduate, a Relentless Search

The deceased, an engineering graduate who had earned a gold medal for academic excellence during his BTech programme, had spent years preparing for government recruitment examinations after completing his degree. According to reports in The Times of India and News18, he attempted at least 50 government job examinations — spanning state and central services — without success.

Family members told police that the young man had grown increasingly despondent in recent months as each examination result arrived without his name on the selection list. Despite his academic credentials, the fiercely competitive nature of India's government recruitment process — where millions of applicants compete for thousands of posts — left him without a placement.

"He used to say, 'I have done everything right, Papa. Why won't they select me?'"

— The victim's father, speaking to local media

India's Unemployment Crisis in Numbers

The tragedy underscores a structural crisis in India's labour market. According to the Centre for Monitoring Indian Economy (CMIE), India's urban youth unemployment rate has hovered near 17 per cent in recent quarters. The problem is particularly acute among degree holders: a 2024 report by the International Labour Organization found that graduates in India are significantly more likely to be unemployed than those with less education — an inversion that speaks to the mismatch between degree production and job creation.

Government positions remain fiercely coveted for their job security, pensions, and social prestige, particularly in states like Uttar Pradesh, where private-sector opportunities outside major cities are scarce. Railway recruitment drives routinely attract tens of millions of applicants for a few thousand posts. The Staff Selection Commission's Combined Graduate Level examination, another popular route, sees pass rates well below 1 per cent.

A Pattern of Despair

The Kanpur case is not an isolated incident. In recent years, a series of suicides linked to examination stress and unemployment have drawn national attention. In July 2026, an 18-year-old NEET aspirant in Faridabad died by suicide after the re-examination results were declared. In Rajasthan, multiple aspirants have taken their lives following paper-leak scandals that invalidated years of preparation.

Mental health professionals say the phenomenon reflects a toxic combination of familial expectations, financial pressure, and a recruitment system that offers few second chances. "These young people stake everything on a single outcome," said Dr Samir Parikh, director of the Department of Mental Health and Behavioural Sciences at Fortis Healthcare. "When the system fails them repeatedly, the psychological toll can be devastating."

What the Diaspora Should Know

For Indians abroad, the story carries a particular resonance. Many in the diaspora left India precisely because of the limited opportunities the domestic job market offered. The suicide highlights the conditions that continue to drive outward migration — and the human cost borne by those who stay behind, unable or unwilling to leave.

The incident has also prompted calls from diaspora groups for greater investment in India's mental health infrastructure and for reforms to the government recruitment process, including faster filling of vacancies and transparent, leak-proof examination systems.

What's Next

Police in Kanpur have registered a case and are investigating the circumstances of the death. Opposition politicians in Uttar Pradesh have seized on the case to demand accountability from the state government over unfilled vacancies and delayed recruitment cycles.

The central government has pledged to fill 10 lakh (one million) government vacancies on a "mission mode" basis, but progress has been slow. Until the pipeline of secure employment catches up with the aspirations of India's educated youth, stories like this one — and the quiet desperation behind the words "Sorry papa, I tried" — are unlikely to stop.
